requirement: A living colony in the leaf litter. Follow the moving leaves.
fact: Leafcutter workers carry plant fragments underground, where the colony uses them as growing material for a cultivated fungus. The fungus becomes their food crop, making the moving leaves the visible edge of an insect agricultural system.
signal: A pheromone—a chemical signal shared among members of a species—connects the colony with a foraging route that human eyes cannot ordinarily detect.
uncertainty: Fungus cultivation and chemical trail behavior are sourced; colony size and the trail's visible geometry are stylized.

requirement: Support native stems to 60% and retain at least 50% canopy. Chemical vision leads to the hidden stem.
fact: Treehoppers communicate through plant-borne vibrations rather than relying only on airborne sound. A living stem becomes a communication channel, carrying motion between insects hidden on different parts of the plant.
signal: A patterned duet travels down the stem. A duet is a coordinated exchange in which one signal is answered by another.
uncertainty: Vibrational communication is documented. Exact Monteverde occurrence, host identity, elevation, and the visual pattern need field review. Numerical habitat rules are game abstractions.

requirement: In lower montane forest, restore flowering cover to 65%. Listen for activity among the stems.
fact: Bombus ephippiatus is a Central American bumblebee. Many bees detect ultraviolet wavelengths beyond human vision, so a flower can present different contrast and information to a bee than it does to us.
signal: Ultraviolet translation reveals contrasting flower regions sometimes described as nectar guides. A visible pattern alone does not prove how this particular bee will behave.
uncertainty: Taxonomy and ultraviolet sensitivity in bees are supported. This species-specific flower pattern and local association are not verified; the earlier vibration cue is a game convention.

requirement: Upper montane: retain 65% canopy and 60% flowering cover. Look beneath a leaf in UV vision; this resting adult opens the night layer.
fact: This tiger moth produces rapid ultrasonic clicks that interfere with a hunting bat's echolocation. Echolocation uses outgoing calls and returning echoes to locate objects; the moth's defense disrupts that sensory information.
signal: Rapid moth clicks overlap the bat's sweeping pulse. This strategy is called sonar jamming, translated here into visible pulses and slowed synthetic sound.
uncertainty: Sonar jamming is experimentally documented. Placement at this cloud-forest elevation is provisional, and the audible sound is a translation rather than a field recording.

requirement: At night in upper montane forest, maintain 65% moisture and 55% deadwood. Ultrasound makes the concealed movement legible.
fact: The scarab's metallic appearance comes partly from microscopic organization in its cuticle, the insect's outer covering. These structures interact with light to produce color and unusual polarization properties rather than relying only on pigment.
signal: A later optical study resolves the shell into shifting bands that translate the orientation of reflected light.
uncertainty: Optical structure is studied. The game does not claim that this species sees circular polarization. Its locating sound, habitat thresholds, and elevation are interpretive.

requirement: Restore flowering cover to 65% in premontane forest, then follow fragrance in chemical vision.
fact: Male orchid bees collect environmental fragrances. Their scent world reveals relationships that are easy to miss with sight alone.
signal: A fragrant plume curls from flower to bee.
uncertainty: Fragrance behavior is supported at the orchid-bee group level; the exact blend and local flower partners are not specified.

requirement: Restore native host stems to 65%, canopy to 55%, and moisture to 50%. Tend the resulting larva for eight game days, then document the adult.
fact: Morpho helenor larvae have been recorded on several host plants in Costa Rica. A caterpillar is the larval feeding stage; it grows through instars between molts, forms a pupa, and later emerges as an adult through complete metamorphosis.
signal: Blue flashes reveal the adult that began beneath the host leaf. Its notebook history preserves Egg → Caterpillar → Pupa → Adult as stages of the same individual.
uncertainty: ACG documents this species, larvae beneath leaves, host records, and life stages. Eight-day development and generic host planting are compressed game rules, not rearing instructions.

requirement: At the elfin ridge, use polarization with canopy at 55% or more. This is a second behavioral plate of the golden scarab, not an additional species.
fact: A familiar animal becomes a new discovery in another sensory world. The ridge study records the shell's changing optical signature.
signal: Rotating bands reveal an animal against the open sky.
uncertainty: Ridge placement and the visualization are interpretive. A distinct color morph or separate species is not claimed.
